1:
That God remembered Noah is agreed to be an expression after the manner of men; the interest lies in what it describes. Henry calls it an act of God's grace and reads it against the emptied world: the whole race of mankind, except Noah and his family, was now driven into the land of forgetfulness, so that God's remembering Noah was the return of his mercy to mankind, of whom he would not make a full end. Divine justice had been answered by the ruin of those sinners, and his spirit was quieted — he remembered mercy in wrath, remembered the days of old, remembered the holy seed, and then remembered Noah. Gill turns it toward Noah's experience: God cannot forget his creatures, but this is said as it might have seemed to Noah, who, having heard nothing for five months, might begin to think himself forgotten — whereas God remembered him and his covenant, and may be said to remember him particularly when he began to take measures for removing the waters. Calvin refers the word not only to the outward aspect of things but to the inward feeling of the holy man. Since the ark floated to the fifth month, the delay by which the Lord suffered his servant to be anxiously and miserably tortured might well seem a kind of oblivion; and Noah might infer that his life had been prolonged only that he might be more miserable than the rest of mankind — for we are accustomed to imagine God absent except when we have some sensible experience of his presence.

The means God used gets a natural explanation from two witnesses. Clarke takes it for such a wind as produced a strong and sudden evaporation, and reports that the effects of these winds, frequent in the east, are truly astonishing — instancing a friend who, bathing in the Tigris near Ctesiphon, was caught by one of the hot winds the natives call samiel. Ellicott is more interested in what the verb concedes: the waters, he renders, became still, which shows that their strength at the close of the previous chapter refers to the violent currents, lasting to the end of the hundred and fiftieth day and then ceasing. The wind, which he compares to the creative wind moving over the waters at the beginning, must have begun as soon as the rains ceased, or even before, given so vast a disturbance of the atmosphere; but its special purpose of assuaging the waters began only when the downpour was over.

How long all this took is disputed, and Calvin gives both reckonings. Some think the whole time from the beginning of the deluge to the abatement is noted here, and so include the forty days of rain; but Calvin holds that until the fortieth day the waters rose gradually, then remained nearly in the same state for a hundred and fifty days, both computations making a little more than six months and a half. He notes that if the seventh month be numbered from the year's beginning rather than from Noah's entering the ark, the subsidence came after five months afloat. And he draws a purpose from its sheer length: by so lengthened a space the Lord would show the more plainly that the desolation had not fallen on the world accidentally, but was a remarkable proof of his judgment, while Noah's deliverance was a magnificent work of his grace. Wesley describes the ebb in a phrase — the waters were going and returning, a gradual departure, the sun's heat exhaling much and the subterraneous caverns perhaps soaking in more. Gill adds a rabbinic note: Jarchi observes that it is not said all the fountains were stopped, as it was said all were broken up, because some were left open for the world's use, and some must remain for the waters to return into.
4:
The date is precise and the reckoning is disputed. Gill takes it for five months after the flood began, and insists it is not the seventh month of the flood but of the year: reckoned from Tisri, it must be Nisan, answering to part of March and part of April, which is how the Targum of Jonathan explains it. But Jarchi makes it Sivan, part of May and part of June, counting the seventh month from Cisleu, when the forty days' rain ceased, and Lightfoot follows him; while Usher fixes the day as Wednesday the sixth of May. Ellicott confirms the arithmetic from the calendar, since the months had each thirty days, so that the interval is exactly a hundred and fifty days; he takes the seventh civil month for Abib, and passes on a set of coincidences noticed in the Speaker's Commentary — that on the seventeenth of Abib the ark rested on Ararat, on the seventeenth of Abib the Israelites passed over the Red Sea, and on the seventeenth of Abib Christ rose again from the dead.

Where Ararat was is a second question, and the two who take it up reach opposite conclusions. Clarke reports that Ararat was a mountain of Armenia is almost universally agreed, and that what is commonly taken for the Ararat of Scripture has been visited by many travellers and carries several monasteries. For a long time, he says, the world has been amused with reports that the remains of the ark were still visible there, but Tournefort, a famous French naturalist who was on the spot, assures us that nothing of the kind is to be seen; and since there is a great chain of mountains called by this name, it is impossible to determine where on them the ark rested, though the highest, called by some the finger mountain, has been fixed on as likeliest — things Clarke thinks of very little consequence. Ellicott doubts the identification altogether. If the received rendering is right that the descendants of Noah travelled from the east to Shinar, this could not be the Ararat of Armenia; the word in Assyrian means highland and may signify any hilly country; and in the Chaldean Genesis the ark rests upon Nizir, east of Assyria, whose highest peak, now named Elwend, is called in the cuneiform texts the mountain of the world. He concedes that the rendering from the east is by no means certain, many translating eastward instead.

Henry attends to what the resting meant to the men inside. It was some satisfaction to Noah to feel the house he was in upon firm ground and no longer movable; and it rested upon a mountain whither it was directed, not by Noah's prudence, for he did not steer it, but by the wise and gracious providence of God, that it might rest the sooner. From which Henry takes his note: God has times and places of rest for his people after their tossings, and many a time provides for their seasonable and comfortable settlement without their own contrivance and quite beyond their own foresight. The tops of the mountains appeared like little islands above the water, and Henry observes that they must have been seen by Noah and his sons, since there were none besides to see them; it is probable they had looked through the window every day, like longing mariners after a tedious voyage. Wesley uses the same interval for a calculation he takes from Lightfoot: they felt ground above forty days before they saw it, from which, if the waters decreased proportionably, it follows that the ark drew eleven cubits of water.
6:
Henry asks why Noah had to discover the flood's ebb for himself, when its coming had been told him to a day. Knowing of the flood's arrival was necessary to his preparing the ark and settling himself in it, whereas knowing of its departure would have served only to gratify his curiosity, so that concealing it was the needful exercise of his faith and patience; and while he could not foresee the flood except by revelation, he might discover its decrease by ordinary means, and God left him to use them. Calvin reads the same delay as evidence of what Noah was feeling. We may conjecture with what anxiety the breast of the holy man was oppressed, since after perceiving the ark to rest on solid ground he still did not dare open the window till the fortieth day — not because he was stunned and torpid, but because an example so formidable of the vengeance of God had affected him with such fear and sorrow that, deprived of all judgment, he silently remained in the chamber of his ark. Gill supplies the date, reckoning the forty days from the first of the tenth month to the eleventh day of the eleventh month, the month Ab, which Usher fixes as Friday the twenty-eighth of August.

Whether the raven ever came back divides the witnesses, and the Hebrew is the battleground. Clarke insists that the common supposition, that the raven flew off and was seen no more, is a meaning the Hebrew text will not bear, since the words say that it went forth, going forth and returning. From which it is evident she did return, though not taken into the ark: she made frequent excursions, continued on the wing as long as she could, picking up such aliment as floated on the waters, and then regained the ark to rest, where she might perch though not be admitted — which must be allowed, since it is impossible she could have kept the wing twenty-one days. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way, noting that the Hebrew says the raven, the particular raven known from this circumstance, and that it went out and returned until the earth was dry without being taken back, the mountain tops and floating carcases affording it both perch and food. Ellicott adds a reason for the choice of bird, and a rival tradition. The raven was chosen as strong of flight, perhaps also as anciently regarded prophetic of the weather, and because easily tamed — and since Noah retained its mate he had security for its return each night to its old perch near the female. But the Chaldean Genesis agrees with many commentators and the ancient versions that the raven did not return, having found abundant food in the floating dead bodies.

The dove is the more delicate instrument, and Gill explains why her failure told Noah more than the raven's success. She feeds on seeds picked off the ground and loves cleanness, and so could find nowhere to alight and have food and yet keep clean; for though the mountain tops were clear of the waters, they might well be muddy with what the waters had left upon them. She therefore returned, and not merely to the ark, as the raven had, but into it. Wesley traces the three sendings and the week between each: the first was probably seven days after the raven, the second seven days after that, the third seven days later still. She came back the first time with no good news, and probably wet and dirty; the second time she brought an olive leaf in her bill which appeared freshly plucked off, a plain indication that the trees were now beginning to appear above water — and Wesley adds what the sign afterwards became, since the olive branch is an emblem of peace.
13:
Henry marks the day as a festival. All the water was now carried off the ground, and Noah was himself an eye-witness of it on the first day of the first month — a joyful new year's day it was. He removed the covering of the ark, not the whole covering, but so much as would suffice to give him a prospect of the earth about it, and a most comfortable prospect he had, for behold, behold and wonder, the face of the ground was dry. Henry draws two notes from it. It is a great mercy to see ground about us, and Noah was more sensible of that than we are, since mercies restored affect us more than mercies continued. And the divine power which now renewed the face of the earth can renew the face of an afflicted troubled soul, and of a distressed persecuted church, making dry ground appear even where it seemed to have been lost and forgotten. Wesley repeats the point in a clause, that Noah removed not the whole covering but so much as would give him a prospect of the earth about him.

Ellicott lays the whole sequence out as a table and draws two conclusions from it. Counting the flood's beginning in Marchesvan, the five months of prevailing water, the seventy-three days before the mountain tops appeared, the forty days before the raven, and the three weekly sendings of the dove, he finds that the day named here falls exactly a month after the bird was last let go. What strikes him is the pace: it was thus very slowly that the earth returned to its normal state. His second inference is drawn from the sevens rather than the totals — the regular weekly interval between the sending forth of the birds proves that the division of time into weeks was already fully established, and suggests besides that religious observances were connected with it. Henry separates the two stages the chapter distinguishes, since the ground was seen to be dry on new year's day but was not habitable for nearly two months more. Wesley states the second stage in a clause, that the earth was dried so as to be a fit habitation for Noah; and Gill records that the Septuagint adds the words 'in the first month' to the opening notice of the year.

That Noah was in the ark a full solar year is agreed, but the three who show their working reconcile the calendar differently. Clarke holds the ancient Hebrew months to have been lunar, the first six of thirty days and the latter six of twenty-nine, so that the twelve fall short of the sun by eleven; and those eleven are exactly the interval between his entering on the seventeenth of the second month and his coming out on the twenty-seventh, which brings the total to a complete solar revolution. Gill reaches the same figure by the same route and then doubts the premise, since it seems very plain to him that the months reckoned here ran to thirty days apiece, the season of prevailing water being counted from the seventeenth of one month to the seventeenth of another. He adds that the month was Marchesvan, as the Targum of Jonathan has it, answering to part of October and part of November, and that Usher fixed the day as Friday the eighteenth of December. Ellicott splits the difference with a suggestion about how the reckoning was kept: thirty days to a month is reasonably certain, yet lunar months fall short of that, so probably the day of the new moon was often counted twice over, as the last of the old and the first of the new. He notes too that the word rendered dried here differs from the one used in the previous verse, marks a further stage, and should be rendered thoroughly dry.
15:
Henry fastens on the one fact that governs the whole section, that Noah did not stir till God bade him. As he had a command to go into the ark, so, however tedious his confinement there had been, he would wait for a command to come out of it again. From which Henry draws the rule: we must in all our ways acknowledge God, and set him before us in all our removes, since those only go under God's protection who follow God's direction and submit to his government. Those who steadily adhere to God's word as their rule, who are guided by his grace as their principle, and who take hints from his providence to help them apply general directions to particular cases, may in faith see him guiding their motions in their march through this wilderness. And Henry adds the consolation that answers the delay — though God detained him long, at last he gave him his discharge, for the vision is for an appointed time, and at the end it shall speak, and shall speak truth, and shall not lie.

Calvin praises the same restraint and anticipates the objection to it. Though Noah was not a little terrified at the judgment of God, his patience is to be commended in this, that having the earth before his eyes, which offered him a home, he yet does not venture to go forth. Profane men may ascribe such waiting to timidity, or even to indolence; but holy is that timidity which is produced by the obedience of faith, and Noah was restrained by a hallowed modesty from allowing himself to enjoy the bounty of nature until he should hear the voice of God directing him to do so. Moses winds the matter up in a few words, Calvin says, but the thing itself deserves attention: all ought spontaneously to consider how great must have been the fortitude of a man who, after the incredible weariness of a whole year, when the deluge has ceased and new life has shone forth, does not yet move a foot out of his sepulchre without the command of God.

Gill fills in the manner of the command and the manner of the obedience. Whether God spoke in a dream or vision, or by an articulate voice appearing in human form, or by an impulse on the mind, is not certain; but he spoke so that Noah heard and understood him, and it was no doubt very rejoicing to Noah, since he had not heard that voice for a year or more, at least that we read of. Though the earth was now dry and fit to be inhabited, he would not go out without orders, as he had not gone in without them. On the command to bring out the creatures Gill notes a various reading: by the margin, as Jarchi observes, the sense is to order them to come forth, and by the text, if they will not, to oblige them. And Noah went forth obedient to the divine command, no doubt with great pleasure in his countenance and a heart full of thankfulness for so great a deliverance, all the creatures going out with him and not one left behind. Calvin hears in the same command a word of comfort, since by it the Lord would cheer the mind of Noah and inspire him with confidence that a seed had been preserved in the ark which should increase till it replenished the whole earth. The renovation of the earth is promised to him, to the end that he may know that the world itself had been enclosed in the ark, and that the solitude and devastation at the sight of which his heart might faint would not be perpetual.
20:
Henry notices that this is the first thing Noah does without being told. Hitherto he had done nothing without particular instructions from God, having had a call into the ark and another out of it; but altars and sacrifices being already of divine institution, he did not stay for a command to express his thankfulness. Those who have received mercy should be forward in returning thanks, not of constraint but willingly, since God is pleased with free-will offerings. Henry then sets the act against the circumstances: Noah was turned out into a cold and desolate world, where one would think his first care would be a house for himself, and behold, he begins with an altar for God — for God, who is the first, must be first served, and he begins well who begins with God. Gill puts the contrast in a sentence: Noah built not a house for himself and his family but an altar for God, his first concern being God's glory and not the temporal good of himself and his. Wesley notes that the beasts and fowls offered were the odd seventh of every clean kind which the earlier chapter had provided.

Clarke makes the altar a hinge of the history. Adam, Cain and Abel had offered sacrifices and can hardly have done so without altars, but this is certainly the first on record; and as the old world began with sacrifice, so did the new. Religion, the proper mode of worshipping the Divine Being, is God's own institution, and sacrifice, in act and design, is the essence of it — without sacrifice, actually offered or implied, there never was and never can be any religion. Its design is twofold: the slaying and burning of the victim shows the sinner's life forfeited to divine justice, and his soul deserving the fire of perdition. He reports without deciding the Jewish tradition that Noah built where Adam's altar had stood, which Cain and Abel used, and where Abraham afterwards offered up Isaac. Gill reports it too and rejects it, calling it not at all probable that the altar Adam raised on leaving Eden was demolished by the flood and rebuilt here; much likelier, he says with Aben Ezra, that Noah built on one of the mountains of Ararat, near where he left the ark.

Ellicott uses the verse against a critical theory. The account of this sacrificial act is said to be an interpolation of the Jehovist, but it forms an integral portion of the numerous flood traditions — for in the Chaldean Genesis, after the sending forth of a dove, a swallow and a raven, the survivor says he sacrificed a sacrifice and built an altar on the peak of the mountain. This antiquity of sections ascribed to the Jehovist, and supposed to be an afterthought, he judges seriously detrimental to the whole theory. He also explains why an altar was needed at all: the flood had swept away all traces of the earthly paradise and of Adam's later home, and Noah had probably been carried far from his own by the floating of the ark, so that to him it was a new earth, with no holy places and no spots hallowed by the past. In consecrating it he gave future generations a sanctuary round which their religious ideas would group themselves. Calvin explains what such offerings were for: they were instituted from the beginning that men might habituate themselves by such exercises to celebrate the goodness of God. The bare confession of the tongue, or even the silent acknowledgment of the heart, might suffice for God, but we know how many stimulants our indolence requires; and it was right besides that they should have symbols before their eyes to admonish them that they had no access to God but through a mediator — though now the manifestation of Christ has taken away these ancient shadows.
21:
The sweet savour is handled carefully, because taken flatly it says something none of the witnesses will allow. Ellicott renders the Hebrew a smell of satisfaction, the idea being not that the sacrifice gave God pleasure but that it caused him to regard man with complacency: the anger at sin which had caused the flood was over, and there was peace between heaven and earth. Calvin is blunter. Moses calls that by which God was appeased an odour of rest, as if to say the sacrifice had been rightly offered; yet nothing can be more absurd than to suppose God appeased by the filthy smoke of entrails and flesh, and Moses here, after his manner, invests God with a human character to suit the capacity of an ignorant people. Nor was the rite in itself grateful to God as a meritorious act; we must regard the end of the work and not the external form, for what else did Noah propose than to acknowledge that he had received his life, and the animals' lives, as the gift of God's mercy alone? That piety, Calvin says, breathed a good and sweet odour before God. Gill takes it as a savour of rest and refers it forward, the sacrifice being offered in the faith of Christ's — a satisfaction to God's justice, an appeasing of his wrath, a propitiation for the sins of men.

On the promise itself the interest falls on small words. Clarke renders the verb as I will not add to curse the ground, meaning there shall not be another deluge to destroy the whole earth; and he reads the clause about man's heart concessively — although that imagination should be evil, that is, should men become as evil afterwards as before, God will not destroy the earth by a flood. He adds the qualification that keeps this from being a reprieve from judgment altogether: God has other means of destruction, and the next time he visits by a general judgment, fire is to be the agent. Ellicott dwells on the phrase said in his heart, in the Hebrew to his heart, meaning that Jehovah determined with himself and came to a settled purpose. Calvin makes the phrase carry weight of another kind: although God never retracts what he has openly spoken with his mouth, we are more deeply affected to hear that he has fixed on something in his own mind, because an inward decree of that kind depends in no way upon creatures.

The reason given for the promise is the reason that had been given for the flood, and both Ellicott and Wesley stop on the difficulty. Ellicott states it as a critical charge: there seems at first sight an inconsistency, and the Jehovist is accused of contradicting the Elohist, since in the earlier place man's inborn sinfulness aggravates his offence, while here it is a reason for mercy. His answer is that the Bible characteristically states the two sides of every principle with abrupt simplicity, most heresies having arisen from seizing one side and omitting the other. In the antediluvian world, with death indefinitely postponed, those imaginations went unrestrained and led to habitual and inveterate sin, so that justice at last smote it; but where man strives against them, and sin is the result of infirmity, mercy heals and grace strengthens the penitent. Wesley finds the difference in a single word. There the imagination of man's heart is said to be evil continually, meaning that his actual transgressions cry against him, whereas here it is evil from his youth, so that he brought it into the world with him. One would think it should follow that the guilty race be wholly extinguished; instead the conclusion is that God will no more take this severe method, since man is rather to be pitied, and such conduct is what might be expected from so degenerate a race.
22:
Both Gill and Clarke hear a limit in the opening clause rather than a guarantee. Clarke finds something very expressive in the original, which reads until all the days of the earth: God does not reckon its duration by centuries, and the words themselves afford a strong presumption that the earth shall not have an endless duration. Gill draws the same conclusion: as to its substance the earth may remain for ever, but as to its form and quality it will be changed, and it and all in it will be burnt up — for the original says as yet all the days of the earth, which shows that a time is fixed for its continuance, and that the time is short, being measured out in days.

How many seasons the verse names is disputed, and Clarke stands alone. Most European nations, he observes, divide the year into four parts, but there are six divisions in the text, probably all intended to describe the seasons of one of these postdiluvian years, and particularly in Armenia, where Noah was when the promise was given. He supports the reading from the calendars: the Targum of Jonathan gives seed-time in September at the autumnal equinox, harvest in March at the vernal, winter beginning at the December solstice and summer at the June, while the Copts reckon their autumn from mid-September. Ellicott calls the six-season reading untenable, and refutes it from the agriculture: in Palestine itself there are two seed times, the winter crops being put into the ground in October and November and the summer crops in January and February. Calvin is blunter still, holding that the Jews erroneously divide their year into six parts, whereas Moses, by setting summer in opposition to winter, divides the whole year in a popular manner into two — and by cold and heat designates those same periods, while by seed-time and harvest he marks the advantages which flow to men from a moderated temperature of the atmosphere.

What the promise secures is read as the restoration of an order the flood had suspended. Calvin says that by these words the world is again completely restored, so great having been the confusion and disorder which overspread the earth that some renovation was necessary — which is why Peter speaks of the old world as having perished in the deluge. The flood had been an interruption of the order of nature itself: the revolutions of the sun and moon had ceased, and there was no distinction of winter and summer; and the Lord here declares it to be his pleasure that all things should recover their vigour and be restored to their functions. Calvin also meets the objection that this equable temperament is not perceived every year: the order of the world is disturbed by our vices, so that many of its movements are irregular, the sun withholding its proper heat, snow or hail following in the place of dew, the air agitated by tempests. Gill supplies what the year in the ark had been like: there had been no seedtime nor harvest, and it must have been mostly damp and cold, so that the difference of the seasons was not discernible — nor even of day and night at times, when the clouds were so black over the heavens that neither sun nor moon nor stars could be seen. Ellicott states positively what the alternations are: the great changes on which the earth's well-being depends, whether taken absolutely, as of light and darkness or cold and heat, or with reference to man's labours, as of sowing and harvesting, or relatively to vegetation, winter being the earth's rest and summer its activity. He records Delitzsch's suggestion that these promises probably came to Noah as strong inward convictions in answer to his prayers during the sacrifice.
